nameStory: Licorice bedstraw gets its name from the sweet, licorice-like scent its roots release when crushed or broken. The "bedstraw" part comes from the old tradition of stuffing mattresses with dried bedstraw plants, whose rough stems and leaves would hold together to create a springy, aromatic filling. Legend says that the Baby Jesus was laid on a bed of sweet-smelling bedstraw in the manger!
description: Licorice bedstraw is a sprawling woodland plant that grows 1-3 feet tall with a loose, open appearance. Its most distinctive feature is its whorled leaves - groups of 4 oval leaves arranged in circles around square stems, creating a neat geometric pattern up the plant. Small, inconspicuous greenish-white flowers cluster along the stems in summer, followed by tiny round fruits. This native perennial has a weedy, informal growth habit and spreads by underground roots to form colonies in shady forest areas.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Four oval leaves arranged in perfect circles (whorls) around the stem at regular intervals, each leaf 1-3 inches long with three prominent parallel veins running lengthwise

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Square stems that feel rigid and slightly rough to the touch, growing in a loose, open pattern that often leans against other plants for support

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny greenish-white flowers in small clusters along the stems, so small they're easy to miss - each flower is barely 1/8 inch across with four petals

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round, bristly fruits that feel slightly sticky and catch on clothing, turning brown when ripe

idTips.label: Root Scent
idTips.description: Roots smell distinctly sweet and licorice-like when crushed or broken - this scent is strongest in fall and spring

habitat: Licorice bedstraw thrives in rich, moist woodlands throughout New England, particularly in deciduous and mixed forests with deep leaf litter. Look for it along shaded forest paths, in woodland clearings, and at forest edges where it gets dappled sunlight. It prefers well-drained but moisture-retentive soils and often grows alongside wild ginger, mayapple, and other woodland wildflowers.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges with fresh green whorled leaves that are perfect for identification. The distinctive leaf arrangement and square stems become clearly visible as the plant reaches full height.
seasonality.summer: Tiny flowers bloom from June through August, though they're easily overlooked. This is when the plant is at full size and most obvious in the woodland understory.
seasonality.fall: Fruits ripen and the root's licorice scent becomes strongest. Leaves may begin to yellow but the plant structure remains intact for identification.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only the underground root system. The plant is not identifiable during winter months.

funFact: Despite being called "wild licorice," this plant is completely unrelated to true licorice (which comes from a Mediterranean legume) - but indigenous peoples of North America independently discovered that the roots taste remarkably similar and used them as a sweet treat and cough remedy for centuries before European contact!
confusionNotes: Licorice bedstraw can be confused with other bedstraws, but most have narrower, more numerous leaves per whorl - licorice bedstraw consistently has just 4 broad, oval leaves per whorl. Memory trick: "Four fat leaves make licorice sweet" - the broader leaves and sweet-scented roots separate it from its skinny-leaved cousins.
contextualKnowledge: The name "wild licorice" can be confusing since this plant belongs to the coffee family (Rubiaceae), not the pea family like true licorice. Some field guides also call it "forest bedstraw" or "white licorice," but all refer to the same species with the distinctive four-leaf whorls and licorice-scented roots.
compareHints: Among New England's 15+ bedstraw species, licorice bedstraw stands out with its consistently four broad, oval leaves per whorl - most others have 6-8 narrow, linear leaves arranged in circles. Catchweed bedstraw has similar leaf numbers but feels much more scratchy and grabby, while sweet woodruff has broader leaves but typically shows 6-8 per whorl. The licorice scent of the roots is also unique among our regional bedstraws.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's bedstraws, catchweed is unique for its extremely clingy nature and annual growth habit.

Hedge bedstraw differs from other common bedstraws by its smooth stems and purely white flowers - catchweed bedstraw has sticky stems, lady's bedstraw has yellow flowers, and fragrant bedstraw has a sweet vanilla scent when crushed.
Unlike its weedy cousin catchweed bedstraw which grabs onto your clothes with hooked bristles, sweet woodruff stays put and feels soft to touch.
Among New England's bedstraws, fragrant bedstraw is unique for its sweet vanilla scent when crushed – most other bedstraws are odorless or have different scents.
Marsh-bedstraw is distinguished from other bedstraws by its preference for consistently wet habitats and its delicate, mat-forming growth pattern.
Lady's bedstraw stands out among New England's bedstraws because of its bright yellow flowers - most other bedstraw species have white or greenish blooms.
Among New England's bedstraws, rough bedstraw is distinguished by its prominent stem hooks and preference for wet areas.
Unlike catchweed bedstraw with its velcro-like sticky stems or sweet woodruff's hay-like fragrance, Torrey's wild licorice has smooth stems and that distinctive taste.
Unlike catchweed bedstraw which has sticky, grabby stems and four-petaled flowers, three-petal bedstraw feels smoother and has its distinctive three-petaled blooms.
Among the 15+ bedstraw species in New England, stiff marsh bedstraw is one of only two with 3-petaled flowers (the other being three-petal bedstraw).
Among New England's bedstraws, hairy bedstraw is unique for its consistently soft, fuzzy texture throughout the plant.

White bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and smooth stems - catchweed bedstraw has hooked bristles that grab onto clothing, while lady's bedstraw has bright yellow flowers instead of white.
Unlike the common catchweed bedstraw with its grabby, rough stems, boreal bedstraw is soft and non-sticky.
Northern bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and narrow leaves with three parallel veins.
Among New England's bedstraws, bluntleaf bedstraw stands out for its preference for wet habitats and those distinctive rounded leaf tips.
